Newborn Care

A breast lump during breastfeeding: getting it checked

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Most breast changes during breastfeeding have a benign explanation, but a new or persistent lump should be assessed. You can usually have the necessary diagnostic tests while continuing to breastfeed; treatment advice depends on what the tests show.

Breastfeeding does not rule out breast cancer

A new lump during breastfeeding often has a non-cancerous explanation, but it still deserves attention. Breast cancer can occur during lactation, and normal fullness or tenderness can make a change harder to recognise. Being young or producing milk does not exclude it.

Your age, personal and family history and the particular change help guide assessment. A general statistic about cancer around pregnancy cannot calculate the chance that an individual lump is malignant. The useful response is to have a new or unexplained change assessed, while remembering that a referral or a scan does not mean cancer has been diagnosed.

Mastitis can cause a tender, swollen area

Mastitis refers to inflammation in breast tissue. It can produce pain, warmth, swelling and skin colour changes, sometimes with fever or flu-like symptoms. Bacterial infection can develop, but inflammation is not automatically an infection or simply a solid plug that must be forced out.

Feeding support can help assess attachment, pumping patterns and oversupply. Avoid deep massage or repeatedly pumping to “empty” the breast, which can worsen inflammation. Seek clinical advice for significant symptoms, fever or a worsening pattern. If antibiotics are prescribed and there is no improvement within the advised interval, contact the clinician again rather than continuing to treat every persistent lump as ordinary mastitis.

An abscess needs drainage and medical care

A breast abscess is a collection of pus. It can appear as a painful swollen area that feels hot, sometimes with fever or feeling unwell. It may follow mastitis, but its development is not evidence that someone failed at breastfeeding or deliberately left a problem untreated.

Assessment usually includes ultrasound, and treatment may involve drainage with a needle or a small incision, sometimes alongside antibiotics. Feeding or gentle expression can often continue with suitable advice about comfort, the wound and the baby’s contact with it. A painful warm lump needs prompt review. If symptoms have not started to improve within about two days of antibiotics, or worsen sooner, seek reassessment.

Fibroadenomas and milk-filled cysts are other possibilities

A fibroadenoma is a benign growth of glandular and fibrous tissue. It can feel smooth or mobile and may enlarge during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Once a diagnosis is established, observation is often appropriate; growth, discomfort or uncertainty may lead to further tests or treatment.

A galactocele is a milk-retention cyst. It may be painless, but large or infected cysts can cause problems and sometimes need drainage. A round, movable or painless lump is not proof of either diagnosis. Cancer can have variable features too, so touch alone cannot reliably separate a benign lump from a malignant one.

Look for changes beyond a distinct lump

Tell a clinician about new skin dimpling or an orange-peel texture, a change in breast shape or size, persistent localised pain, a new nipple inversion or a lump in the armpit. A nipple rash that persists, particularly on one side, also needs attention.

Milk discharge is expected during lactation, but spontaneous bloody or otherwise unusual discharge should be discussed. Redness, darkening, warmth or swelling may be inflammation or another condition; redness can be less visible on darker skin. None of these signs proves cancer, and the absence of pain does not exclude it. A change that persists or keeps returning deserves a clear explanation.

Do not wait for weaning or a fixed one-week deadline

Arrange a prompt appointment for a new, unexplained or persistent breast lump. A lump that enlarges, recurs in the same place after treatment, feels fixed or is accompanied by skin or nipple changes should not be left until breastfeeding ends. You do not need to wait exactly a week before asking for help.

Describe when it began, whether it changes after feeding and any fever, pain, discharge or previous treatment. Mention personal and family breast-cancer history. If the breast is hot and painful or you feel unwell, seek urgent advice. Severe illness, confusion, fainting or breathing difficulty requires emergency assessment; an infection can also become serious.

Imaging can be done while you are breastfeeding

Ultrasound is often used to examine a palpable lump and can help show whether it is fluid-filled or solid. Mammography may provide additional information, and MRI may be appropriate for selected questions. Lactation changes the appearance and density of the breast, so tell the imaging service that you are breastfeeding.

Necessary breast imaging should not be postponed for routine weaning. Feeding or expressing shortly before the appointment may improve comfort and image assessment. Ordinary ultrasound and mammography do not make milk radioactive. MRI contrast and other tests should be discussed using the specific agent and procedure; nuclear-medicine tracers are a different issue from a standard breast scan.

A biopsy may be needed to establish the diagnosis

If imaging or the examination leaves concern, a core needle biopsy can take a small tissue sample for laboratory assessment. Having a biopsy recommendation does not mean cancer has already been confirmed. It is a way to obtain an answer when appearance alone is insufficient.

Core biopsy with local anaesthetic is generally compatible with lactation, and routine interruption of breastfeeding is usually unnecessary. Tell the team about medicines and allergies, and ask about wound care and follow-up. A small risk of milk leakage or bleeding should be discussed, but it should not become a reason to indefinitely delay an indicated biopsy.

Surgery and feeding need a procedure-specific plan

If cancer is diagnosed, surgery may remove the tumour and surrounding tissue or the whole breast. The choice depends on the cancer and treatment plan. A breast that has been removed cannot produce milk; after both breasts are removed, breastfeeding is no longer possible. Some people can feed from the unaffected breast after one-sided treatment.

Cancer surgery should not be delayed simply to finish weaning. Ask about the operation, anaesthetic, pain medicines and any dye or radioactive tracer used to assess lymph nodes. These details determine whether any temporary interruption is needed. “Pump and dump” is not a universal rule after surgery, and keeping or reducing milk production should be planned with the breast and lactation teams.

Chemotherapy and other systemic treatments may require stopping breastfeeding

Cytotoxic chemotherapy can pass into milk and harm an infant, so breastfeeding is generally not compatible during treatment. Feeding only from the breast without cancer does not solve this problem: a medicine circulating in the body can reach milk from either side.

Endocrine treatments and newer targeted or immune therapies also need a specific review; some are incompatible and others lack adequate safety information. The oncology team should explain when feeding must stop and whether or when restarting could be considered after the final dose. Do not invent a waiting interval from the drug’s name or skip cancer treatment to continue breastfeeding.

Radiotherapy changes the plan for the treated breast

During radiotherapy directed at a breast, current breast-surgery guidance advises against feeding or pumping from that side. The team can plan a reduction in milk production before treatment and help manage discomfort. Feeding from the other breast may be possible if the rest of the treatment is compatible.

Radiation can reduce later milk production and affect the skin and breast tissue, but its effects are not identical for everyone. Ask for specialist advice about future feeding from the treated side. Do not assume that every form of radiation treatment has the same precautions: external-beam breast treatment and treatments involving radioactive substances require different instructions.

Support recovery and make room for uncertainty

Treatment can cause fatigue, weakness, pain, nausea or weight changes. Practical help with infant care, feeding, meals and travel to appointments can make treatment more manageable. A lactation professional can help with maintaining suitable feeding or gradually reducing production, and the child’s clinician can help arrange adequate alternative nutrition.

Breast cancers in younger or recently postpartum patients can have challenging features, but age alone does not determine the outcome. Prognosis depends on the tumour’s biology, stage and response to treatment. Prompt investigation avoids preventable delay. If feeding needs to change, that is a medical care decision, not a failure; ask for emotional support as well as a clear treatment plan.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

The feel of a lump and lactation status cannot establish whether it is benign.

Diagnostic imaging and biopsy generally do not require weaning; cancer treatment needs a specific feeding plan.

How BeMama can help

Bring a short history of the lump, any treatment and feeding changes, and ask who will communicate the results and follow-up plan.

When to seek help

Seek prompt assessment for a new, persistent or recurrent lump or skin/nipple change. A hot painful breast with fever or feeling unwell needs urgent advice; severe systemic illness requires emergency care.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Breastfeeding does not exclude cancer.
  • Mastitis, abscess, fibroadenoma and galactocele are different conditions.
  • A smooth or movable lump still needs an appropriate diagnosis.
  • Do not postpone indicated tests until weaning.
  • Surgery, systemic medicines and radiation have different feeding implications.

Frequently asked questions

Does breastfeeding mean a lump cannot be cancer?

No. Many lumps are benign, but breast cancer can occur during lactation. A new, persistent or unexplained change needs assessment rather than reassurance from breastfeeding status alone.

Can I tell that a lump is harmless because it moves?

No. Smoothness, mobility and absence of pain are not reliable diagnostic tests. Examination and imaging, sometimes followed by a biopsy, establish the cause.

Is mastitis always a bacterial infection?

No. Mastitis includes inflammation that may occur without bacterial infection. Management depends on the findings, and deep massage or excessive pumping can worsen the problem.

What if a lump returns in exactly the same place?

Arrange reassessment, particularly after previous treatment. A recurring or persistent area may need imaging rather than repeated assumptions that it is a blocked duct.

Do I have to stop breastfeeding before ultrasound or mammography?

Usually not. These tests are compatible with lactation. Tell the service you are breastfeeding and ask whether feeding or expressing shortly before the appointment would help.

Does a needle biopsy require pumping and discarding milk?

Not routinely. A core biopsy with local anaesthetic is generally compatible with continued feeding. Follow the team’s specific wound-care and medicine advice.

Can I feed from the other breast during chemotherapy?

Generally no during cytotoxic chemotherapy. The medicines circulate through the body and may enter milk from both breasts. The oncology team must confirm any restart interval.

Can breastfeeding continue during breast radiotherapy?

Feeding or pumping from the treated side is generally avoided during treatment. The unaffected side may be an option if other medicines are compatible. Plan this with the oncology and lactation teams.

Will removing one breast always end breastfeeding?

The removed breast cannot make milk, but feeding from the remaining breast may be possible. The full treatment plan and the child’s nutritional needs determine what is feasible.

Should I wait a week to see whether a new lump goes away?

There is no requirement to wait a fixed week. Arrange prompt advice for an unexplained lump, and seek urgent care sooner for a hot painful breast, fever or feeling unwell.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
